newsitem.title: USA: AOL reaches pact on pricing with 20 states.
newsitem.headline: AOL reaches pact on pricing with 20 states.

text.p: America Online Inc. reached an agreement with 20 state attorneys general over its new flat rate pricing plan, with AOL agreeing to pay automatic refunds to its subscribers who do not want to pay $19.95 a month.
Last month, the world's largest online service announced a new pricing plan of unlimited access for $19.95 a month, vs. its previous plan of $9.95 a month for five hours.
On Dec. 1, AOL automatically switched all subscribers to the new plan, unless members notified AOL that they did not want the new plan.
Many states said this practice was deceptive, because the change was implemented "in a manner that was misleading."

The agreement was announced by Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger and filed in Suffolk Superior Court, a state court, in Boston. Nineteen other attorneys general took part in the agreement.

The other states included Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Hawaii, Iowa, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, Vermont, Wisconsin, and the territory of Guam. Last week, the state of Washington announced its own similar agreement with America Online.
America Online officials were not immediately available to comment.
"Today's agreement secures automatic funds for AOL members who do not want the company's more expensive flat-rate plan," Harshbarger said in a statement.

According to its agreement with the states, AOL must obtain affirmative consent to the billing change from as many of its 7 million members as possible. For example, a "pop-up" screen will request that members either agree to the new plan or pick another billing option.
AOL must automatically provide retroactive refunds to all consumers who ask to switch back to their old plan before March 31, 1997.

AOL will provide a toll-free number to handle inquiries and complaints regarding the new flat-rate service and AOL must notify its members of their rights and obligations regarding the automatic conversion plan through the U.S. mail and in a series of online screens.

"The common sense principles of consumer protection do not end in cyberspace," said Harshbarger in a statement. "Companies should not be allowed to change the terms of an agreement with their customers in ways that make it difficult for them to understand or accept the new terms."
AOL's stock rose 12.5 cents to $40 on the New York Stock Exchange.
